A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same survey, Recent Advances in Speech Language Models. The complete text, equations, figures, tables, and references support reliable comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

before.justification: v1 synthesizes cited research and provides illustrative task examples. It reports no original experimental, simulation, user-study, or empirical data-analysis outcomes.

after.justification: v2 remains a literature survey. Its additional model descriptions, benchmark catalog, and post-alignment findings are attributed to other work, without original empirical results.

M1.justification: Neither version introduces a proposed executable model or algorithm. v2 expands descriptions of surveyed methods and clarifies continuous representations already discussed in v1; these are documentation and literature-coverage changes.

E1.justification: v2 catalogs additional datasets and benchmarks, including Multilingual LibriSpeech, VoxCeleb2, VoiceBench, and VoxEval. Neither version actually trains or evaluates a model on these resources, so this expands survey coverage rather than experimental dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Changes to the architecture catalog do not constitute evaluated baseline changes. Retained literature comparisons use the same alternatives, including GSLM's CPC, wav2vec 2.0, and HuBERT comparison and AudioPaLM's w2v-BERT, USM-v1, and USM-v2 comparison.

E3.justification: v2 adds descriptions of real-time interaction measures and speech-output benchmarks in Section VI-A, but does not apply them in an experiment. Neither PDF reports an experimental protocol conducted for this survey.

E4.justification: No ablation, robustness experiment, or case study is added or revised. v2 describes interruption assessments and VoxEval's varied audio conditions without presenting corresponding analysis results.

E5.justification: The descriptions of pGSLM's 20 generated samples and prosodic standard deviation remain unchanged. Neither version reports seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates for original results.

E6.justification: Section IV-B3 adds cited qualitative findings: Align-SLM identifies inconsistent responses to identical prompts, and SpeechAlign observes poor acoustic quality associated with generated-token mismatch. Existing GSLM and AudioPaLM rankings remain unchanged. These additions are literature findings, not original measurements.

T1.justification: Section III-A explicitly adds s = v for continuous tokens alongside the quantized definitions given in v1. Continuous features were already discussed conceptually, making this a limited extension of the formal description. The numbered equations otherwise retain their substance; no proofs are added.

C1.justification: v2 adds latency reduction as a central advantage over ASR + LLM + TTS in the abstract and introduction, alongside the retained information-loss and cumulative-error arguments. The four headline survey contributions remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of design trade-offs: continuous-feature storage and training costs, semantic versus paralinguistic effects of text alignment, and latency versus reasoning and stability during inference. It also explains limitations of text-output benchmarks and narrows the separate-component-training generalization to some studies.

D1.justification: v2 adds a companion survey-repository link in the abstract footnote, absent from v1. This supplies new resource-access information without documenting a new experimental implementation.

R1.justification: Coverage expands substantially to post-alignment through Align-SLM and SpeechAlign, newer models including Parrot and OmniFlatten, and evaluation resources including VoiceBench and VoxEval. v1's stated absence of post-alignment research is replaced by a dedicated subsection. Some earlier coverage, including VALL-E and Wav2Prompt, is removed.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify tokenization, codecs, and introductory motivation. Silence mode becomes interactive period recognition, and post-alignment receives a subsection. The eight main sections retain their order, and much of the existing prose remains unchanged.

P2.justification: Tables 1–4 become Tables II–V, with revised architecture and dataset catalogs. v2 adds notation Table I and benchmark Table VI, updates Figure 3, and changes the dataset table from full-width to single-column. IEEE-style typography, headings, captions, and reference layout substantially alter the presentation.

improvement.justification: The added post-alignment coverage, clearer treatment of continuous representations, and expanded benchmark guide make the survey more current and useful. These gains outweigh localized editorial problems, including duplicated interactive-period-recognition prose and Table VI's incorrect SUPERB citation. The central survey framework remains largely intact, supporting a limited net improvement.
